questions.q:
At a school fair stall in Pune, three flasks of tea are kept. A thermometer shows flask 1 at 78 °C, flask 2 at 65 °C and flask 3 at 52 °C. Volunteers who touch the outside of the flasks call all three 'hot'. The stall rule is to serve tea only from 60 °C to 70 °C, both included. Each flask cools by about 2 °C every 5 minutes.
(a) Which flask can be served right now?
(b) What will each flask read after 20 minutes?
(c) Why did the volunteers call all three 'hot' although the readings differ so much?
(d) At the 20-minute mark, which flask should the stall serve, and for about how many more minutes can it keep serving that flask before it leaves the band? Use (b).
questions.a: (a) Flask 2 only (65 °C); flask 1 is above 70 °C and flask 3 is below 60 °C. (b) Each falls about 2 x 4 = 8 °C: flask 1 to 70 °C, flask 2 to 57 °C, flask 3 to 44 °C. (c) Touch can tell that something is hot but cannot give a reliable measure; it cannot show a 26 °C gap between flasks, while temperature can. (d) Serve flask 1, which is now at 70 °C, inside the band; flask 2 has dropped below 60 °C. Flask 1 must fall 10 °C more to reach 60 °C; at 2 °C every 5 minutes that takes about 25 more minutes.
s: Flask 2 only, at 65 °C, with the other two outside the band
Readings after 20 minutes: 70, 57 and 44 °C
Touch cannot measure the difference; temperature is the reliable measure
Serve flask 1; about 25 more minutes (10 °C at 2 °C per 5 minutes)

questions.q: Tenzin fills three bowls: P with warm water, Q with tap water and R with ice-cold water. He keeps his right hand in P and his left hand in R for two minutes, then puts both hands into Q at the same time. What will he most likely feel?
questions.a: His right hand feels the water in Q as cool, while his left hand feels the same water as warm
o: His right hand feels the water in Q as cool, while his left hand feels the same water as warm
His right hand feels the water in Q as warm, while his left hand feels the same water as cool
Both hands feel the water in Q as equally lukewarm, because it is ordinary tap water
Both hands feel the water in Q as cool, because tap water is colder than warm water

questions.q: True or False? 'If one bucket of water feels cold to my hand and another feels warm, the cold-feeling bucket must be at a lower temperature.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. What the hand feels depends on what it touched just before; the same water can feel cold after warm water and warm after ice-cold water. Only a thermometer reading can show which bucket is at the lower temperature.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: touch depends on what the hand touched before; the same water can feel cold or warm, so a thermometer is needed

questions.q: A school's water tank reads 18 °C at 6 am and 31 °C at 3 pm on Monday. On Tuesday it reads 21 °C at 6 am and 30 °C at 3 pm. On which day did the tank water warm up more between 6 am and 3 pm, and by how much more?
questions.a: Monday, by 4 °C more (13 °C against 9 °C)
o: Monday, by 4 °C more (13 °C against 9 °C)
Tuesday, because its 6 am reading of 21 °C is the higher one
Monday, by 1 °C more, because 31 °C is 1 °C above 30 °C
Both days equally, because both end at about 30 °C

questions.q:
Statement 1: A body at 30 °C is hotter than a body at 25 °C.
Statement 2: If two bodies feel equally warm to touch, they must be at the same temperature.
Statement 3: The difference in temperature between two bodies tells us how hot one body is compared with the other.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 2 only
All three statements

questions.q: After the three-bowl activity, Kabir says: 'The water in the middle bowl changed. It cooled down for my right hand and warmed up for my left hand.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. The water in the middle bowl stayed at one temperature; a thermometer would show the same reading throughout. Only the feeling differed: his right hand came from warm water, so the middle water felt cool; his left hand came from ice-cold water, so it felt warm. The activity shows that touch cannot always judge hotness correctly.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
The water's temperature did not change; a thermometer would read the same
The different feelings come from where each hand had been, showing touch is unreliable

questions.q: Dolly comes home after playing in the afternoon sun. Her grandmother touches Dolly's forehead and says she has a fever. Her brother measures her temperature with a clinical thermometer and finds it normal. Which judgement is best?
questions.a: Trust the thermometer, because touch alone cannot always judge hotness correctly
o: Trust the thermometer, because touch alone cannot always judge hotness correctly
Trust the grandmother, because touching is direct while a thermometer only guesses
Trust neither, because a forehead warmed by the sun shows the body is hotter than any reading
Distrust the thermometer, because a feverish forehead always feels warm

questions.q:
In the three-bowl activity, bowl A is at 42 °C, bowl B at 26 °C and bowl C at 7 °C.
(a) By how many degrees is A hotter than B, and by how many degrees is B hotter than C?
(b) Using your answer to (a), explain why a hand taken from A feels B as cool while a hand taken from C feels B as warm.
questions.a: (a) A is 16 °C hotter than B; B is 19 °C hotter than C. (b) The hand from A comes from water 16 °C hotter than B, so B feels cool; the hand from C comes from water 19 °C colder, so B feels warm. B is at 26 °C for both hands; the feeling depends on where the hand was before.
s: Differences 16 °C (A minus B) and 19 °C (B minus C)
Feeling explained by where each hand came from, with B's temperature the same for both

questions.q: Which of these situations does NOT show that our sense of touch can mislead us?
questions.a: Two bowls both read 30 °C on a thermometer, so a girl says they are equally hot
o: Two bowls both read 30 °C on a thermometer, so a girl says they are equally hot
After holding an ice pack, a boy finds room-temperature water feels warm
After a long hot bath in winter, a girl finds the tap water feels very cold
After carrying a cold bottle, a boy says plain water in a cup feels warm

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Tea at 82 °C is 16 °C hotter than tea at 66 °C, even though both cups feel 'too hot to sip' to the same person.
Reason (R): The difference in temperature between two bodies tells us how hot one body is in comparison to the other.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Four students each kept a hand for two minutes in a different bowl and then touched the same bottle of water, which a thermometer showed to be at 25 °C. Their bowls and reports were: Arjun 50 °C, 'cool'; Bina 35 °C, 'cool'; Chetan 15 °C, 'warm'; Divya 5 °C, 'warm'.
(i) For each student, was the earlier bowl hotter or colder than the bottle, and by how many degrees?
(ii) What pattern links the bowl to the report?
(iii) Did the bottle's temperature change from student to student? Give a reason.
(iv) Two students called the same bottle 'cool' and two called it 'warm'. Is any of them lying? Explain.
(v) What conclusion should the class write?
questions.a: (i) Arjun's bowl was 25 °C hotter, Bina's 10 °C hotter, Chetan's 10 °C colder, Divya's 20 °C colder. (ii) A hand from a hotter bowl called the bottle cool; a hand from a colder bowl called it warm. (iii) No; the thermometer showed 25 °C, one reading for everyone. (iv) No one is lying; each reported what the hand felt, and the feeling depends on where the hand had been. (v) We cannot always rely on touch to judge hotness; temperature read on a thermometer is the reliable measure.
s: All four differences with hotter or colder: 25, 10, 10, 20 °C
Pattern: hotter bowl gives 'cool', colder bowl gives 'warm'
Bottle stayed at 25 °C, shown by the single thermometer reading
Reports are honest feelings that depend on the earlier bowl
Conclusion: touch is unreliable, temperature is reliable

questions.q:
A boy's temperature reads 38.6 °C at 8 am and 38.2 °C at noon. His mother touches his forehead at noon and says, 'He feels just as hot as this morning, so the fever has not changed.'
(a) Has his temperature changed? State what the two readings show.
(b) Why could her hand not tell her this?
questions.a: (a) Yes. It fell by 0.4 °C, from 38.6 °C to 38.2 °C, though he still has a fever. (b) Touch cannot give a reliable measure of hotness; a change of less than half a degree is far too small for a hand to judge, while a thermometer shows it as a number.
s: Temperature fell by 0.4 °C (still above normal)
Touch is not a reliable measure and cannot detect so small a change; the thermometer can

questions.q: In a sweet shop, a thermometer gives these readings: freezer air -18 °C, ice cream in a display box -12 °C, a glass of iced water 0 °C and tap water 27 °C. Which order runs from the COLDEST to the HOTTEST?
questions.a: Freezer air, ice cream, iced water, tap water
o: Freezer air, ice cream, iced water, tap water
Ice cream, freezer air, iced water, tap water
Iced water, ice cream, freezer air, tap water
Tap water, iced water, ice cream, freezer air

questions.q:
On a summer afternoon Neha touches tap water and then water from a matka, and correctly says the matka water is cooler.
(a) Why could touch give her the right answer this time?
(b) Describe one change to what her hand did just before, which could make the same matka water feel warm to her.
questions.a: (a) Both samples were touched by a hand in the same condition, and the difference between them was large enough to notice, so touch happened to give the right order. (b) If she had first kept that hand in ice-cold water for a minute or two, the matka water could feel warm, because what the hand feels depends on what it touched just before.
s: Touch can work when the hand starts in the same condition and the difference is large
A hand taken from ice-cold water first would feel the matka water as warm

questions.q:
A bowl of dal is served for lunch and a thermometer in it reads 72 °C at 1:00, 61 °C at 1:10, 53 °C at 1:20 and 47 °C at 1:30.
(i) In which ten minutes did the dal cool the most, and by how many degrees?
(ii) By how many degrees did it cool in all from 1:00 to 1:30?
(iii) A cup of water beside it reads 50 °C at 1:30. Which is hotter at 1:30, the dal or the water, and by how much?
questions.a: (i) 1:00 to 1:10: it fell 72 - 61 = 11 °C (then 8 °C and 6 °C in the next two ten-minute periods). (ii) 72 - 47 = 25 °C. (iii) The water: 50 - 47 = 3 °C hotter. A higher temperature means a hotter body, and the difference tells how much hotter.
s: 1:00 to 1:10, a fall of 11 °C (against 8 °C and 6 °C)
Total fall 25 °C
The water is hotter, by 3 °C

questions.q: Glass A of milk reads 64 °C and glass B reads 41 °C; both feel 'too hot to hold' to Kiran. Ten minutes later A has fallen by 15 °C and B by 6 °C. Which statement is correct now?
questions.a: A is still hotter than B, now by 14 °C
o: A is still hotter than B, now by 14 °C
B is now hotter than A, because B lost fewer degrees
A is still hotter than B, by 23 °C as at the start
A and B are now equally hot, because both have lost heat

questions.q:
Asha's mother is filling a bucket for her baby brother's bath. She has just washed dishes in water at 48 °C. Testing the bath water with the same hand, she finds it 'only a little warm'. A bath thermometer in the bucket reads 41 °C. The family doctor has told them to keep bath water between 36 °C and 38 °C.
(a) Why did the 41 °C water feel only a little warm to her?
(b) By how many degrees is the bath water above the doctor's upper limit?
(c) Which was more reliable here, her hand or the thermometer? Give a reason.
(d) Asha says, 'Testing with the hand is fine if the hand has not just been in other water.' Her mother says, 'Use the thermometer every time.' Whose rule would you adopt? Justify using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) Her hand came from water at 48 °C, 7 °C hotter, so the bath water felt less warm than it was. (b) 41 - 38 = 3 °C. (c) The thermometer; touch cannot always judge hotness correctly, as (a) shows. (d) The mother's rule: Asha is partly right that a rested hand avoids this particular error, but the safe band is only 2 °C wide (36-38 °C) and touch gives no number, so only the thermometer can show the water is inside it.
s: Hand came from 48 °C water, 7 °C hotter, so the bath felt only a little warm
3 °C above the upper limit of 38 °C
Thermometer more reliable, because touch can mislead
Justified choice weighing Asha's point against the narrow 2 °C band that touch cannot judge

questions.q:
Phiban walks home in the cold Shillong rain, gripping an icy metal umbrella handle. At home she touches her brother Lambok's forehead and he feels hot to her, but the thermometer shows his temperature is normal.
(a) Using the three-bowl activity, explain why her hand may have misled her.
(b) Why was taking out the thermometer still the right step, even though it found nothing wrong?
questions.a: (a) Her hand had just been very cold, like the hand taken from ice-cold water in the activity, so a body at normal temperature felt warm to it. (b) Touch cannot always judge hotness correctly, so her feeling needed a check; the thermometer gives a reliable measure, and a normal reading is itself useful information.
s: Cold hand makes a normal forehead feel hot, as with the hand from ice-cold water
Thermometer gives the reliable reading that checks the unreliable feeling

questions.q:
Work backwards. A bowl of water reads 30 °C. You want a friend's RIGHT hand to feel this water as cool and her LEFT hand to feel the same water as warm.
(i) Suggest a temperature for the water each hand should be kept in first, and say why.
(ii) What will a thermometer show for the 30 °C bowl when each hand is in it?
(iii) Could a right hand taken from water at 20 °C feel the 30 °C bowl as cool? Give a reason.
questions.a: (i) Any suitable pair: the right hand first in water clearly hotter than 30 °C (for example 45 °C) and the left hand first in water clearly colder than 30 °C (for example 10 °C), because a hand coming from hotter water feels the bowl as cool and a hand coming from colder water feels it as warm. (ii) The same reading, 30 °C, for both; the water's temperature does not depend on whose hand is in it. (iii) No. Coming from colder water, the hand would feel the 30 °C water as warm, not cool.
s: Right-hand bowl above 30 °C and left-hand bowl below 30 °C, with the reason
Thermometer reads 30 °C either way
A hand from 20 °C water feels it warm, so 'cool' is not possible

questions.a: (i) Warm kettle water in one outer bowl, matka water in the other outer bowl and tap water in the middle bowl: the middle bowl must be between the other two, hotter than the matka water and colder than the warm water. (ii) Keep the right hand in the warm water and the left hand in the matka water for 1-2 minutes, then put both hands into the tap water together. (iii) The right hand will feel the tap water as cool and the left hand will feel it as warm. (iv) Repeat with the hands swapped: the left hand will now feel the tap water as cool, so the feeling follows the earlier bowl, not the hand. (v) Read the thermometer in the tap water: one reading, the same whichever hand is in it. Conclusion: we cannot always rely on touch to judge hotness; temperature measured with a thermometer is reliable.
s: Tap water in the middle bowl, between the warm and the matka water, with the reason
Method: hands in the outer bowls 1-2 minutes, then both into the middle bowl
Prediction: cool to the hand from warm water, warm to the hand from matka water
Swap the hands to show the earlier bowl, not the hand, decides the feeling
One thermometer reading for the middle bowl; touch unreliable, temperature reliable

questions.q: True or False? 'In a healthy family measured at the same time with the same thermometer, the grandmother reads 36.6 °C and her five-year-old grandson reads 37.3 °C. At least one of them must be unwell.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. 37.0 °C is only the average body temperature of many healthy people, and body temperature is influenced by factors such as age, time of day and activity level. Both readings are close to 37.0 °C, so both can be normal for healthy people.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: 37.0 °C is an average and age is one factor that changes body temperature, so both can be normal

questions.q: Farhan, who feels perfectly well, washes his hands and the thermometer tip, presses reset, places the digital thermometer under his tongue and closes his mouth. Ten seconds later, while the display is still changing, he takes it out, reads 34.1 °C, and then washes and dries the tip. Which step explains why his record cannot be his body temperature?
questions.a: Taking it out before it beeped or flashed, while still changing
o: Taking it out before it beeped or flashed, while still changing
Pressing reset first, which wipes out the temperature it should measure
Closing his mouth, which stops the tip from sensing the body
Washing the tip before use, which leaves it cooled by the water

questions.q:
Rohan uses a digital clinical thermometer like this: (1) he reads the instruction manual first; (2) he cleans the thermometer by dipping the whole thing, display and all, into soapy water; (3) he hands it to his sister holding it by the tip.
(a) Which of his three actions follow the precautions and which break them?
(b) Rewrite each action that breaks a precaution so that it follows it.
questions.a: (a) Action 1 follows a precaution (use it after reading the instruction manual). Action 2 breaks one: while washing, the digital portion such as the display must be kept out of water. Action 3 breaks one: the thermometer must not be held by the tip. (b) Wash only the tip with soap and water, keeping the display out of the water, and dry it; pass it on holding the body, not the tip.
s: Action 1 correct; actions 2 and 3 break the display-dry and not-by-the-tip precautions
Rewritten: wash only the tip with the display kept dry, and hold it by the body

questions.q:
A school health room follows one rule: a child whose ACTUAL body temperature is 38.0 °C or more is sent home. Four children are checked. Anu, armpit, 37.6 °C. Babu, armpit, 36.9 °C. Chiru, under the tongue, 38.3 °C. Deepa, armpit, 37.0 °C. The nurse knows the rule about armpit readings.
(a) Should Anu be sent home? Show the range of her actual temperature.
(b) Should Babu be sent home? Show the range.
(c) Why is Deepa's case harder to decide than Babu's?
(d) The nurse has time for one more check. Whom should she re-check, and how? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Yes: actual 38.1 °C to 38.6 °C, at or above 38.0 °C either way. (b) No: actual 37.4 °C to 37.9 °C, below 38.0 °C either way. (c) Deepa's actual temperature is 37.5 °C to 38.0 °C, so it may just reach the 38.0 °C limit; the armpit rule alone cannot settle it. (d) Re-check Deepa under the tongue, which reads the body temperature directly instead of the lower armpit value; Anu, Babu and Chiru are already decided.
s: Anu: 38.1-38.6 °C, sent home
Babu: 37.4-37.9 °C, stays
Deepa: 37.5-38.0 °C straddles the limit
Re-check Deepa under the tongue, with reason

questions.q: A clinical thermometer is used correctly on four different people. Which reading lies outside the band in which human body temperature normally stays?

Assertion (A): For a healthy grandmother, an armpit reading of 36.3 °C is consistent with a normal body temperature of about 37.0 °C.
Reason (R): A temperature taken in the armpit is about 0.5 °C to 1 °C higher than the actual body temperature.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Mohan's digital thermometer reads 36.2 °C under his tongue. He says: 'Thermometers always read lower than the real body temperature, so I must add 0.5 °C to 1 °C. My real temperature is 36.7 °C to 37.2 °C.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No, his claim is wrong. The 0.5 °C to 1 °C correction is real only for a reading taken in the armpit, which is lower than the actual body temperature; thermometers do not 'always' read low. His reading was taken under the tongue, the usual way of measuring body temperature, so nothing is added: his temperature is 36.2 °C. That is above 35 °C and slightly below the 37.0 °C average, which can still be normal for a healthy person.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
The 0.5 °C to 1 °C correction applies only to armpit readings, not to every reading
An under-the-tongue reading is used as it is, 36.2 °C, which can be normal

questions.q:
For five days Sana measures her own temperature under the tongue at 7 am and at 5 pm. Mornings: 36.5, 36.6, 36.4, 36.6, 36.5 °C. Evenings: 37.0, 37.1, 36.9, 37.1, 37.0 °C. She felt well all week.
(a) Compare each evening reading with the same day's morning reading. What pattern do you find?
(b) Which factor that influences body temperature does this pattern point to, and does it mean Sana was ill in the mornings?
questions.a: (a) Each evening reading is 0.5 °C higher than that day's morning reading, every day. (b) Time of day. No: a healthy person's normal temperature can be slightly different from 37.0 °C and can change with the time of day, so the lower morning readings are normal for her.
s: Evening is 0.5 °C higher than morning on all five days
Factor: time of day; the morning readings are still normal

questions.q: During a disease outbreak, railway staff must check the body temperature of hundreds of travellers at a station gate. Which choice suits the job best, and why?
questions.a: Non-contact (infrared) thermometers, since they measure without touching anyone
o: Non-contact (infrared) thermometers, since they measure without touching anyone
Laboratory thermometers, since they have a much wider range than clinical ones
Digital clinical thermometers placed under each traveller's tongue in turn
Mercury clinical thermometers, since they need no batteries to keep working

questions.q:
In a class activity, ten healthy students measured their temperatures under the tongue: 36.8, 37.1, 36.9, 37.3, 36.6, 37.0, 37.2, 36.7, 37.4 and 37.0 (all in °C).
(i) What are the highest and the lowest readings, and the difference between them?
(ii) How many students read exactly 37.0 °C?
(iii) Find the average of the ten readings.
(iv) Do these results support the idea that normal temperature is the average of many healthy people? Explain.
(v) Give two factors that could explain why the readings differ.
questions.a: (i) Highest 37.4 °C, lowest 36.6 °C, difference 0.8 °C. (ii) Two. (iii) Sum 370.0 °C, average 37.0 °C. (iv) Yes: only two of ten read exactly 37.0 °C, yet the average is 37.0 °C, which is what that idea predicts. (v) Any two of age, time of day and activity level.
s: Highest 37.4, lowest 36.6, difference 0.8 °C
Two students at exactly 37.0 °C
Supports 'normal is an average', with the evidence
Two factors from age, time of day, activity level

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with what it tells you in Column II.
Column I
1. 36.4 °C under the tongue of a healthy girl
2. 98.6 °F
3. Crushed ice that is melting
4. 43 °C
Column II
a. Above the band in which human body temperature normally stays
b. Slightly below the 37.0 °C average, and can still be normal
c. Cannot be measured with a clinical thermometer
d. The same temperature as 37.0 °C, on another scale

A healthy, active boy's temperature is measured under his tongue and the display shows 30.5 °C. Show that this cannot be a correct reading of his body temperature, and suggest one mistake that could explain it.
questions.a: Human body temperature does not normally go below 35 °C, and a healthy person is close to 37.0 °C, so 30.5 °C is more than 4 °C below even the lowest normal value; it cannot be his body temperature. A likely mistake: the thermometer was taken out before it beeped or flashed (or was not reset or not kept under a closed mouth).
s: Body temperature normally stays at or above 35 °C
30.5 °C is below that limit, so the reading is impossible for him
A plausible handling mistake, such as reading before the beep

questions.q:
A grandmother's temperature is taken in the armpit with a digital thermometer and reads 34.6 °C. Her grandson says, 'That is below 35 °C, so the reading is impossible.'
(a) Work out the range of her actual body temperature and say whether he is right.
(b) Before anyone decides whether she is well, what should be done about this reading, and why?
questions.a: (a) An armpit reading is about 0.5 °C to 1 °C lower than the actual body temperature, so her actual temperature is about 35.1 °C to 35.6 °C. That is not below 35 °C, so the reading is not impossible; he forgot the armpit correction. (b) Take the temperature again carefully, under the tongue or in the armpit while waiting for the beep, because a single armpit reading that low may come from a wrong method and only gives a range, not her actual temperature.
s: Actual 35.1-35.6 °C, not below 35 °C, so not impossible
Re-measure carefully (under the tongue or wait for the beep), because one armpit reading gives only a range

questions.q: Sita has only a digital clinical thermometer at home. Which of these tasks can she do with it correctly?
questions.a: Measure her mother's temperature under the tongue after washing and resetting it
o: Measure her mother's temperature under the tongue after washing and resetting it
Find the temperature of crushed ice melting in a glass for a project
Check the temperature of water boiling in a kettle for tea
Measure her father's temperature while holding the thermometer by its tip

questions.q:
Find the errors. At a school camp in Ooty, a volunteer checks children with one digital clinical thermometer. Her notes say: 'Kavya: under the tongue, took it out after 10 seconds, no beep yet: 33.8 °C. Between children I wiped the tip on my shirt. At the end I dropped the whole thermometer into a bucket of soapy water to clean it.' Each reading takes about 20 seconds to beep, and washing and drying the tip takes about 15 seconds. Thirty children are still to be checked, and the bus leaves in 15 minutes.
(a) Show that Kavya's recorded value cannot be her body temperature, and name the mistake that explains it.
(b) Name the two cleaning precautions the volunteer broke.
(c) How long would the 30 checks take with and without washing the tip each time?
(d) Should she skip washing the tip to finish before the bus leaves? Use (b) and (c) to justify your decision.
questions.a: (a) Human body temperature does not normally go below 35 °C, and 33.8 °C is below that; she took the thermometer out before the beep, so the reading had not settled. (b) The tip should be washed with soap and water before and after use (not wiped on a shirt), and the display must be kept out of water while washing (not dropped into a bucket). (c) Without washing: 30 x 20 = 600 s = 10 minutes. With washing: 30 x 35 = 1050 s = 17.5 minutes, 2.5 minutes more than she has. (d) No: washing the tip is a precaution because the same tip goes into thirty mouths. Since the full job needs 17.5 minutes, she should keep washing and either ask for a second volunteer and thermometer or finish the last few children after the trip starts, rather than share an unwashed tip.
s: 33.8 °C is below 35 °C; taken out before the beep
Precautions broken: tip not washed with soap and water; display put in water
10 minutes without washing, 17.5 minutes with washing
Keeps washing, with a practical way to cover the 2.5-minute shortfall

questions.q:
Statement 1: Digital clinical thermometers run on batteries.
Statement 2: A non-contact thermometer gives a reading only when it is pressed against the person's skin.
Statement 3: A clinical thermometer can measure the temperature of boiling water if it is left in the water long enough.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Nine-year-old Rahul is ill. His mother records his temperature under the tongue at 8 am and 8 pm for four days. The doctor says that readings within 0.5 °C of 37.0 °C count as normal.
Day 1: 8 am 38.4 °C, 8 pm 38.8 °C
Day 2: 8 am 37.9 °C, 8 pm 38.2 °C
Day 3: 8 am 37.2 °C, 8 pm 37.6 °C
Day 4: 8 am 36.8 °C, 8 pm 37.1 °C
(i) By how much did the highest reading exceed the top of the doctor's normal band?
(ii) His mother says the fever was over on the morning of Day 3. Is the 8 am reading of Day 3 normal, and is her conclusion safe?
(iii) On which day can you say Rahul's temperature had returned to normal? Give a reason.
questions.a: (i) The top of the normal band is 37.0 + 0.5 = 37.5 °C; the highest reading is 38.8 °C (Day 1, 8 pm), so it exceeded the band by 1.3 °C. (ii) 37.2 °C is within 0.5 °C of 37.0 °C, so that reading is normal, but the 8 pm reading on the same day was 37.6 °C, above the band; one normal morning reading does not show the fever is over, so the conclusion is not safe. (iii) Day 4: both readings (36.8 and 37.1 °C) lie within 36.5 °C to 37.5 °C.
s: 37.2 °C is normal but the 37.6 °C evening reading is above the band, so not safe
Day 4, both readings within 36.5-37.5 °C

questions.q:
Grandfather wants to keep using his old mercury clinical thermometer instead of the family's new digital one, because 'mine never needs a battery'. His eyesight is weak.
(a) What is correct in what he says about the digital thermometer?
(b) Mercury thermometers are being replaced by digital ones. Give one way the digital thermometer suits him better, and judge whether 'no battery' outweighs it.
questions.a: (a) Digital clinical thermometers do run on batteries, so he is right that his old one needs none. (b) The digital thermometer shows the temperature as numbers on a display, which are easier to read, and it beeps or flashes when the reading is ready, so with weak eyes he does not have to judge a thin column. Changing a battery now and then is a small cost next to reading his temperature correctly, so 'no battery' does not outweigh it; he should use the digital one.
s: Digital clinical thermometers run on batteries
A digital advantage for him (easy-to-read numbers, beep when ready) judged to outweigh the battery

questions.q: Sunil, a healthy student, runs two rounds of the school ground and at once measures his temperature under the tongue: 37.3 °C. Thirty minutes later, sitting in class, he reads 36.8 °C with the same thermometer used the same way. What is the best interpretation?
questions.a: Both can be normal; activity level influences body temperature
o: Both can be normal; activity level influences body temperature
He had a fever after running, which went away within thirty minutes
The thermometer is faulty, because one person must give the same reading twice
Only 36.8 °C is correct, because any reading above 37.0 °C is a fever

questions.q:
Work backwards. The best answer to a question is: 'Use a non-contact (infrared) thermometer.'
(a) Write a situation (who is checked, where, and how many people) for which this is the best answer.
(b) Give the reason that makes the non-contact thermometer the better choice in your situation.
(c) Change one detail of your situation so that a digital clinical thermometer becomes a sensible choice, and say why.
questions.a: (a) Any suitable situation, for example: guards checking about 500 visitors entering a hospital during an outbreak of a disease. (b) A non-contact thermometer measures temperature without touching anyone, so it reduces the risk of spreading disease when many people are checked one after another. (c) For example: only one sick child is to be checked at home; the digital clinical thermometer, used under the tongue and washed before and after use, gives her temperature, and there is no crowd for disease to spread through.
s: A situation with many people checked, for example at an entrance during an outbreak
Reason: measures without touching, so less risk of spreading disease
Changed detail (one person at home) that makes the digital thermometer sensible, with reason

questions.a: (i) Wash hands and the tip with soap and water, reset, place it under the tongue with the mouth closed, wait for the beep or flash, then read the display. (ii) Clean the tip with soap and water, keeping the display out of the water, and dry it. (iii) The batteries, because digital clinical thermometers run on batteries. (iv) No; 37.0 °C is only the average of many healthy people, and a healthy person may read slightly above it. (v) No; the temperature of boiling water is outside the range of a clinical thermometer.
s: Correct measuring steps, waiting for the beep
Wash and dry the tip, display kept out of water
Check the batteries, since it is battery-run
37.3 °C can be normal: 37.0 °C is an average
Boiling water is outside the clinical range

questions.q:
Find the errors. For a science fair in Bhopal, a Class 6 team makes a poster titled 'How cold can it get?'. Its table reads:
Ice cream in a freezer box: -12 °C
Room: 25 K
Absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature: 0 °C
The team checked the ice cream and the room with a laboratory thermometer marked in degrees Celsius.
(a) Correct the absolute zero line, giving the value in both kelvin and degrees Celsius.
(b) What did the team mean by 'Room: 25 K', and what is the correct value in kelvin?
(c) A visitor finds the gap between the room and the ice cream in kelvin. What does she get, and how does it compare with the gap in degrees Celsius?
(d) The team can fix only one error before judging starts. Which error would mislead visitors more? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Absolute zero is 0 K, which is close to -273.15 °C. (b) They read 25 °C on the thermometer but wrote the wrong unit; 25 °C = 25 + 273.15 = 298.15 K. (c) Ice cream: -12 + 273.15 = 261.15 K; 298.15 - 261.15 = 37 K, the same as 25 - (-12) = 37 °C, because the same 273.15 is added to both. (d) Fix the absolute zero line. It is wrong by about 273 degrees and teaches the opposite of the poster's point, that melting ice is the coldest anything can be, while the ice cream line on the same poster (-12 °C) already sits below it. '25 K' is also wrong, but 25 K would be about -248 °C, colder than the ice cream, so a visitor who compares it with the ice cream line can see it is a slip.
s: Absolute zero: 0 K, close to -273.15 °C
Meant 25 °C; correct value 298.15 K
Gap 37 K, equal to the 37 °C gap
Fix the absolute zero line: off by about 273 degrees and contradicted by the -12 °C line; '25 K' is a slip a visitor can spot

questions.q: A beaker of water in the school laboratory is at 25 °C. It is warmed by 18 °C. A student has to record the new temperature on the Kelvin scale. What should she write?

Rekha measures her own temperature with a digital thermometer. The display shows 98.6 with no unit.
(a) On which scale is it reading, and what is that temperature on the Celsius scale?
(b) If the display had meant 98.6 on the Celsius scale, what would you conclude about the reading? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The Fahrenheit scale; 98.6 °F is the same as 37.0 °C, normal body temperature. (b) The reading would be impossible for a living person, because human body temperature does not normally go above 42 °C.
s: Fahrenheit, equal to 37.0 °C
98.6 °C would be impossible: body temperature normally stays at or below 42 °C

questions.q:
Statement 1: The unit kelvin is written with a capital letter at the start, as 'Kelvin', like the unit 'Celsius'.
Statement 2: A degree sign is not written with K.
Statement 3: A space is left between the number and the unit, as in 40 °C.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Meena says: 'Kelvin is just Celsius plus 273.15, so if one beaker of water is twice as many degrees Celsius as another, it is also twice as many kelvin. Water at 40 °C has twice the kelvin temperature of water at 20 °C.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. 40 °C = 40 + 273.15 = 313.15 K and 20 °C = 20 + 273.15 = 293.15 K. Twice 293.15 is 586.3, not 313.15. Adding the same 273.15 to both numbers keeps the gap the same (20 °C and 20 K) but does not keep 'twice as much'.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Conversions: 313.15 K and 293.15 K
313.15 K is not twice 293.15 K (586.3 K); adding 273.15 keeps the gap, not the ratio

questions.q: Isha's cousin in another country messages: 'My son's temperature is 102 this morning.' She does not name the scale. Which scale does she most likely mean, and why?
questions.a: Fahrenheit, because 102 is a little above the normal 98.6 °F
o: Fahrenheit, because 102 is a little above the normal 98.6 °F
Celsius, because clinical thermometers generally use that scale
Kelvin, because the kelvin is the SI unit of temperature
Celsius, because 102 °C is only slightly above normal

questions.q:
Two groups heat the same kind of water in a school laboratory. Group A records in kelvin: 293.15 K at the start, 318.15 K after 5 minutes and 343.15 K after 10 minutes. Group B records in degrees Celsius: 20 °C, 45 °C and 70 °C at the same times.
(i) Convert Group A's three readings to degrees Celsius.
(ii) Did the two groups record the same temperatures? Explain.
(iii) Find the rise in each 5 minutes, in degrees Celsius and in kelvin.
(iv) If the water keeps rising at the same rate, what would each group write after 15 minutes?
(v) Group B's leader wants the final report in degrees Fahrenheit 'because everyone knows 98.6'. Advise her, with two reasons from what you know about the scales.
questions.a: (i) 293.15 - 273.15 = 20 °C, 318.15 - 273.15 = 45 °C, 343.15 - 273.15 = 70 °C. (ii) Yes; the readings are the same temperatures written on two scales. (iii) 25 °C every 5 minutes, which is also 25 K. (iv) Group B: 70 + 25 = 95 °C; Group A: 343.15 + 25 = 368.15 K (= 95 + 273.15). (v) Advise against it: the Fahrenheit scale is not used in most scientific studies anymore, and the only Fahrenheit value they know is that 37.0 °C equals 98.6 °F, so they have no way to write 20, 45, 70 or 95 °C in °F. Kelvin, the SI unit, or Celsius suits the report.
s: Converts to 20, 45, 70 °C
Same temperatures on two scales
Rise 25 °C = 25 K every 5 minutes
After 15 minutes: 95 °C and 368.15 K
Fahrenheit not used in most scientific work, and only the 37.0 °C = 98.6 °F pair is known

questions.q: A sample of liquid nitrogen in a research laboratory is at 77.15 K. It warms by 100 K. Its temperature is now ___ °C.
True or False? 'When a beaker of water warms up by 15 °C, its temperature has also gone up by 15 K.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The kelvin value is the Celsius value plus 273.15. For example 20 °C = 293.15 K and 35 °C = 308.15 K: the Celsius rise is 15 °C and the kelvin rise is 308.15 - 293.15 = 15 K, because the same 273.15 is added to both readings.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the same 273.15 is added to both readings, so a rise of 15 °C is a rise of 15 K (with an example)

questions.q:
For a science exhibition in Lucknow, a Class 6 team displays four samples with their thermometer readings: chilled water 4 °C, room air 27 °C, hot water 85 °C and freezer air -18 °C. Each label must also show the temperature on the Kelvin scale.
(a) What should the label for the room air say in kelvin?
(b) What should the label for the freezer air say in kelvin?
(c) How many kelvin hotter is the hot water than the freezer air?
(d) The team wants one label to show how far the hot water is above absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature. Is the kelvin value or the Celsius value the better number to print for this? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 27 + 273.15 = 300.15 K. (b) -18 + 273.15 = 255.15 K. (c) Hot water 85 + 273.15 = 358.15 K; 358.15 - 255.15 = 103 K (the same as 85 - (-18) = 103 °C). (d) The kelvin value: 0 K is absolute zero, so 358.15 K is directly how many kelvin the hot water is above absolute zero. The Celsius value, 85 °C, is measured from 0 °C (melting ice), so a visitor would have to add 273.15 to get the same answer.
s: Room air 300.15 K
Freezer air 255.15 K
Difference 103 K
Kelvin, because the Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero (0 K) while Celsius starts at 0 °C

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A beaker reading 25 °C and a beaker reading 298.15 K are equally hot.
Reason (R): The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Arjun says: 'Our laboratory thermometer reads from -10 °C to 110 °C, so its range spans 120 °C. If its scale were relabelled in kelvin, the range would still span 120 K.' Check his claim by converting both ends.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. -10 °C = -10 + 273.15 = 263.15 K and 110 °C = 110 + 273.15 = 383.15 K. Span in Celsius: 110 - (-10) = 120 °C; span in kelvin: 383.15 - 263.15 = 120 K. The spans are equal because the same 273.15 is added to both ends.
s: Verdict: correct
Both ends converted: 263.15 K and 383.15 K
Spans 120 °C and 120 K, equal because the same 273.15 is added to both ends

questions.q: A gas in a laboratory flask is at 310.15 K. It is then cooled by 45 K. Ananya needs the new temperature in degrees Celsius. What is it?

A line in a lab notebook reads: 'The water was at 50°c, the room at 298.15 K and the ice bath at 273.15 °K.'
(a) Which of the three temperatures is already written correctly?
(b) Correct the other two, naming the rule each one breaks.
questions.a: (a) '298.15 K' is correct: a space before the unit and no degree sign with K. (b) '50°c' should be '50 °C': a space must be left between the number and the unit, and the symbol is a capital C. '273.15 °K' should be '273.15 K': the degree sign is not written with K.
s: 298.15 K picked out as correct
50 °C (space, capital C) and 273.15 K (no degree sign with K)

b. 37 °C
