A quiz card lists five temperatures: 300 K, 20 °C, 98.6 °F, 0 K and -5 °C.
(i) Write 300 K in degrees Celsius.
(ii) Write -5 °C in kelvin.
(iii) Arrange all five from the coldest to the hottest.
(iv) Which two of the five are closest to each other, and how far apart are they?
(v) The card's writer says, '98.6 °F is the value a scientist would most likely write in a research paper.' Comment on this.
questions.a: (i) 300 - 273.15 = 26.85 °C. (ii) -5 + 273.15 = 268.15 K. (iii) 0 K (about -273.15 °C), -5 °C, 20 °C, 300 K (26.85 °C), 98.6 °F (37.0 °C). (iv) 20 °C and 300 K (26.85 °C), 6.85 degrees apart; the next closest pair, 300 K and 98.6 °F, is 10.15 degrees apart. (v) Unlikely: the Fahrenheit scale is not used in most scientific studies anymore; scientific work uses the Kelvin scale, whose unit, the kelvin, is the SI unit.
s: Correct order coldest to hottest
20 °C and 300 K, 6.85 degrees apart
Fahrenheit is not used in most scientific studies; kelvin is the SI unit

questions.q: A research group is writing up an experiment for a science journal. Which choice of temperature unit would be the LEAST suitable, and why?
questions.a: Degree Fahrenheit, because that scale is not used in most scientific studies anymore
o: Degree Fahrenheit, because that scale is not used in most scientific studies anymore
Kelvin, because it is written without a degree sign
Degree Celsius, because laboratory thermometers are marked in it
Kelvin, because its scale starts at absolute zero

questions.q: A classmate writes '-20 K' as the temperature of a cold room. Explain why this cannot be right, and give the correct Kelvin value if the room was really at -20 °C.
questions.a: 0 K is absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, so no temperature can be below 0 K and '-20 K' cannot exist. If the room was at -20 °C, the Kelvin value is -20 + 273.15 = 253.15 K.
s: No temperature below 0 K, absolute zero

questions.q: A website claims that a substance was cooled to -280 °C. Show that this cannot be true.
questions.a: Convert to kelvin: -280 + 273.15 = -6.85 K. Absolute zero, 0 K (about -273.15 °C), is the lowest temperature that can be achieved, so a temperature 6.85 K below it cannot exist. The claim is false.
s: Converts -280 °C to -6.85 K
States that 0 K, absolute zero, is the lowest possible temperature
Concludes the claim is impossible

questions.q: A quiz card lists four temperatures said to have been measured in experiments. Which one can NOT be a real temperature?
o: 5 K

questions.q: True or False? 'Liquid nitrogen at -196 °C is far colder than melting ice, yet it is less than 70 degrees above the lowest temperature that can be achieved.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The lowest temperature that can be achieved is absolute zero, close to -273.15 °C (0 K). -196 °C is -196 + 273.15 = 77.15 K, so it is 77.15 degrees above absolute zero, more than 70. (It is indeed far colder than melting ice at 0 °C.)
s: Verdict: False
Correction: -196 °C = 77.15 K, so it is 77.15 degrees above absolute zero, not less than 70

questions.q:
A school receives a laboratory manual that gives every temperature in kelvin: ice bath 273.15 K, room 298.15 K, warm bath 318.15 K, hot bath 353.15 K. The school's laboratory thermometers have a range of -10 °C to 110 °C and their smallest division reads 1 °C.
(a) What is the warm bath temperature in degrees Celsius?
(b) What is the hot bath temperature in degrees Celsius?
(c) Can the school's thermometers measure all four temperatures? Explain.
(d) The manual is for Class 6 students. The teacher can either rewrite every temperature in the manual in degrees Celsius, or leave it in kelvin and have the students convert each value before they start. Which would you advise? Give one point for each choice and then decide.
questions.a: (a) 318.15 - 273.15 = 45 °C. (b) 353.15 - 273.15 = 80 °C. (c) Yes: the four are 0, 25, 45 and 80 °C, all inside -10 °C to 110 °C. (d) Rewrite the manual in degrees Celsius. The thermometers are marked only in °C, so a kelvin value has to be converted in the middle of the experiment, and a slip there (for example setting the hot bath to 53 °C from '353.15') is made with hot water and is not noticed until later. Keeping kelvin does give practice with kelvin = Celsius + 273.15 and uses the SI unit, but that practice can be done on paper before the lesson; the kelvin values can stay in brackets beside the Celsius ones.
s: Warm bath 45 °C
Hot bath 80 °C
All four (0, 25, 45, 80 °C) lie in the range
Rewrite in Celsius: the thermometers read °C and a slip mid-experiment is costly; the SI-unit practice can be done separately

questions.q:
On each thermometer in Column I the top of the liquid column is 3 small divisions above the 20 °C mark. Each thermometer is described by the gap between two bigger marks and the number of small divisions between them. Match it with its reading in Column II.
Column I
1. 10 °C gap, 10 divisions
2. 10 °C gap, 20 divisions
3. 20 °C gap, 10 divisions
4. 50 °C gap, 10 divisions
Column II
a. 26 °C
b. 21.5 °C
c. 35 °C
d. 23 °C

A part of a laboratory thermometer is described. A bigger mark labelled 30 °C is at the bottom of the part and a bigger mark labelled 40 °C is above it. Four small marks between them split the gap into 5 equal divisions. The top of the liquid column is at the third small mark above 30 °C.
(i) What does one small division read?
(ii) What is the reading?
(iii) If the temperature then falls by 4 °C, where will the top of the column be?
questions.a: (i) 10 ÷ 5 = 2 °C. (ii) 30 + 3 × 2 = 36 °C. (iii) 36 - 4 = 32 °C, which is the first small mark above 30 °C.
s: Smallest division 2 °C
Reading 36 °C
32 °C, at the first small mark above 30 °C

questions.q: On Ishita's laboratory thermometer the bigger marks are 5 °C apart, and there are 4 small marks between any two bigger marks. The top of the liquid column is at the third small mark above the 25 °C mark. What is the reading?

Thermometer A has a range of -10 °C to 110 °C and its smallest division reads 1 °C. Thermometer B has a range of 0 °C to 50 °C and its smallest division reads 0.5 °C.
(a) Find the span of the range of each thermometer.
(b) Using (a) and the smallest divisions, which thermometer would you use for water at 46.5 °C, and which for water at 85 °C?
questions.a: (a) A: 110 - (-10) = 120 °C. B: 50 - 0 = 50 °C. (b) 46.5 °C: B, because it lies in B's range and B can read 0.5 °C steps, which A cannot. 85 °C: A, because 85 °C is beyond B's highest mark of 50 °C.
s: Spans 120 °C and 50 °C
B for 46.5 °C (needs 0.5 °C divisions), A for 85 °C (outside B's range)

questions.q:
Three thermometers, P, Q and R, are placed in the same beaker of water. On all three the bigger marks are 10 °C apart. Between two bigger marks, P has 5 small divisions, Q has 10 and R has 20. On R the reading is 23.5 °C.
(a) Find the smallest value each thermometer can read.
(b) On R, how many small divisions above the 20 °C mark is the top of the column?
(c) On P, between which two marks does the top of the column lie?
(d) R's range is 0 °C to 50 °C, while P and Q read -10 °C to 110 °C. A project will warm this water slowly from about 20 °C to 45 °C, recording to the nearest 0.5 °C, and at the end bring it to the boil and record that too. Should the group use one thermometer throughout, or switch? Justify using (a).
questions.a: (a) P: 10 ÷ 5 = 2 °C, Q: 10 ÷ 10 = 1 °C, R: 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 °C. (b) (23.5 - 20) ÷ 0.5 = 7 small divisions. (c) Between the 22 °C and 24 °C marks, since P's marks go up in 2 °C steps. (d) Only R reads 0.5 °C steps, so R is needed for the 20-45 °C part; but boiling water is far above R's top mark of 50 °C, so R cannot take the last reading. Use R for the warming and switch to Q (1 °C, reaches 110 °C) for the boiling reading. Using Q throughout is simpler but fails the 0.5 °C requirement.
s: 7 small divisions
Between 22 °C and 24 °C
Switch: R for 0.5 °C readings up to 45 °C, Q for boiling water beyond R's range

questions.q:
Statement 1: A thermometer whose bigger marks are 10 °C apart, with 4 small marks between them making 5 equal divisions, reads 2 °C per small division.
Statement 2: A thermometer marked from -10 °C at the bottom to 110 °C at the top has a range that spans 120 °C.
Statement 3: When the top of the liquid column is level with the 30 °C mark, the reading is 30 °C, wherever the bulb happens to be on the scale.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only

questions.q:
On a thermometer whose smallest division reads 0.5 °C, the top of the liquid column is 7 small divisions above the 20 °C mark.
(a) What is the reading?
(b) The water warms to 26 °C. By how many small divisions does the top of the column move up from its position in (a)?
s: Reading 23.5 °C
Rise of 2.5 °C = 5 small divisions

questions.a: (i) X: only X reaches 98 °C. (ii) Z: only Z goes down to -20 °C. (iii) Y: 37.5 °C is in its range and only Y reads 0.5 °C steps. (iv) Spans: X 120 °C, Y 50 °C, Z 80 °C, so X is widest. (v) The thermometer with the finest divisions (Y) has the narrowest range, and the widest ranges (X, Z) have coarser divisions, so each task needs a different one.
s: X for boiling water, as only X reaches 98 °C
Z for -20 °C, as only Z goes that low
Y for 37.5 °C, needing 0.5 °C divisions
Spans 120, 50, 80 °C; X widest
Trade-off between range and fineness of divisions

questions.q: A part of a laboratory thermometer is described. A bigger mark labelled 0 °C is at the top of the part and a bigger mark labelled -10 °C is below it. The gap between them is split into 10 equal small divisions. The top of the liquid column is at the fourth small mark BELOW the 0 °C mark. What is the reading?
Thermometer P has 10 small divisions between two bigger marks and thermometer Q has 20. Sonu says, 'Q will always read finer temperatures than P.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. More divisions give a finer reading only if the bigger marks are the same gap apart. If both have bigger marks 10 °C apart, P reads 1 °C and Q reads 0.5 °C, so Q is finer. But if Q's bigger marks are 20 °C apart while P's are 10 °C apart, both read 1 °C. He must also know the gap between the bigger marks.
s: Verdict: partly right
Case where Q is finer: same gap, 1 °C against 0.5 °C
Case where they are equal: Q's gap 20 °C gives 1 °C, so the gap matters too

questions.q: On a laboratory thermometer there are 20 small divisions between the 10 °C mark and the 20 °C mark. The top of the liquid column is 9 small divisions above the 10 °C mark, so the reading is ___ °C.

A cold-storage room for vegetables in Nashik needs a thermometer that reads from -25 °C to 15 °C and can show temperatures to the nearest 0.5 °C. You are asked to design its scale with bigger marks every 5 °C.
(i) What is the span of the range?
(ii) How many small divisions must lie between two bigger marks? Show the division.
(iii) How many bigger marks will the scale carry, and how many small divisions along the whole scale?
(iv) A worker sees the top of the liquid column 3 small divisions below the 0 °C mark. What is the reading?
(v) A manager asks you to save effort by drawing only 5 small divisions between bigger marks. What would the thermometer then read per division, and would it still meet the room's need?
questions.a: (i) 15 - (-25) = 40 °C. (ii) 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10 small divisions between two bigger marks. (iii) Bigger marks at -25, -20, -15, -10, -5, 0, 5, 10 and 15 °C: 9 marks; 40 ÷ 0.5 = 80 small divisions in all. (iv) 0 - 3 x 0.5 = -1.5 °C. (v) 5 ÷ 5 = 1 °C per division; it could no longer show 0.5 °C steps, so it would not meet the need.
s: Span 40 °C
10 small divisions (5 ÷ 0.5)
9 bigger marks and 80 small divisions
Reading -1.5 °C
1 °C per division, which fails the 0.5 °C need

questions.q:
Shabnam is drawing the part of a thermometer scale between 10 °C and 20 °C so that the smallest division reads 0.5 °C.
(a) How many small divisions must she draw between the 10 °C and 20 °C marks?
(b) At which small mark above 10 °C should she write 12.5 °C?
questions.a: (a) 10 ÷ 0.5 = 20 small divisions. (b) 12.5 - 10 = 2.5 °C, and 2.5 ÷ 0.5 = 5, so at the fifth small mark above 10 °C.
s: 20 small divisions
12.5 °C at the fifth small mark above 10 °C

questions.q: A laboratory thermometer has a range of -10 °C to 110 °C. Which of these could it NOT be used to measure?
questions.a: A salt and ice mixture at about -15 °C
o: A salt and ice mixture at about -15 °C
Water boiling at about 98 °C
Ice that is melting in a beaker at 0 °C
Warm water in a beaker at about 45 °C

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A clinical thermometer is the right choice for measuring the temperature of boiling water in the laboratory.
Reason (R): Laboratory thermometers typically have a range from -10 °C to 110 °C.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: True or False? 'Two laboratory thermometers with the same range can have different smallest divisions.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The range only tells the lowest and highest temperatures marked. The smallest division depends on how many small divisions lie between two bigger marks, which can differ, e.g. both may read -10 °C to 110 °C but one has 10 divisions per 10 °C (1 °C) and the other 20 (0.5 °C).
s: Verdict: True
Reason: smallest division depends on the number of divisions between bigger marks, not on the range

questions.a: (i) E.g. bigger marks 10 °C apart with 5 small divisions (10 ÷ 5 = 2 °C). (ii) E.g. bigger marks 5 °C apart with 10 small divisions. (iii) 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 °C. (Other correct pairs are accepted, e.g. 10 °C with 20 divisions.)
s: A gap and number of divisions giving 2 °C
A gap and number of divisions giving 0.5 °C
Division shown to check (ii)

questions.q:
A school in Bhopal needs 10 laboratory thermometers and has Rs 1,350. Type A costs Rs 120 and reads -10 °C to 110 °C with 1 °C divisions. Type B costs Rs 180 and reads 0 °C to 50 °C with 0.5 °C divisions. This year's experiments are: measuring boiling water, measuring tap water, and measuring warm water to the nearest 0.5 °C. Glass thermometers break if they hit something hard, and last year one was broken.
(a) What would 10 type A thermometers cost, and how much money would be left?
(b) If the school buys some of each, what is the largest number of type B it can buy and still get 10 thermometers in all? What do they cost?
(c) Which of the three experiments can type B NOT do, and why?
(d) Should the school buy 10 of type A, or the mix from (b)? Justify using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) 10 x 120 = Rs 1,200, leaving Rs 150. (b) Each type B in place of a type A adds Rs 60; Rs 150 allows 2 such swaps (3 would need Rs 180). So 8 type A and 2 type B: 960 + 360 = Rs 1,320. (c) Boiling water: its temperature is above B's highest mark of 50 °C. (d) Buy the mix. With ten of type A, no thermometer reads 0.5 °C, so one of this year's three experiments cannot be done at all; the mix covers all three, using type A for boiling water and type B for the 0.5 °C readings. The Rs 150 left by ten type A is tempting as money for a replacement, but a breakage is only a risk, which handling with care reduces, while the lost experiment is certain. The cost of the mix is that groups must take turns with two type B and only Rs 30 is left.
s: Rs 1,200, Rs 150 left
8 type A and 2 type B, Rs 1,320
B cannot measure boiling water: above its 50 °C top mark
Buy the mix: ten type A make the 0.5 °C experiment impossible, while a breakage is only a risk

questions.q: Ankit borrows a thermometer from another school and reads it as if each small division were 1 °C, as on his own thermometer. Explain the risk, and say what he should check before using it.
questions.a: Thermometers in different laboratories may have different ranges and smallest divisions, so his readings could be wrong (e.g. double the true change if each division is really 0.5 °C). He should first find its range and work out the smallest division: the gap between two bigger marks divided by the number of small divisions between them.
s: Risk: range and smallest division can differ, so readings may be wrong
Check: range, and smallest division = gap between bigger marks ÷ number of divisions

questions.q: Karthik must measure a beaker of water that he expects to be at about 36.5 °C, to the nearest 0.5 °C. Which of these thermometers should he choose?
questions.a: Range 0 °C to 50 °C, smallest division 0.5 °C
o: Range 0 °C to 50 °C, smallest division 0.5 °C
Range 0 °C to 30 °C, smallest division 0.5 °C
Range -10 °C to 110 °C, smallest division 1 °C
Range -30 °C to 50 °C, smallest division 2 °C

questions.q:
Gaurav studies a laboratory thermometer. Its lowest mark is -20 °C and its highest is 120 °C. The bigger marks are at -20, 0, 20, 40 and so on, and there are 10 small divisions between any two bigger marks.
(i) State its range.
(ii) Find the span of the range.
(iii) Find the smallest value it can read.
(iv) The top of the liquid column is 5 small divisions above the 60 °C mark. What is the reading?
(v) Can a mark on this thermometer show 71 °C? Explain.
questions.a: (i) -20 °C to 120 °C. (ii) 120 - (-20) = 140 °C. (iii) 20 ÷ 10 = 2 °C. (iv) 60 + 5 × 2 = 70 °C. (v) No. The marks go up in 2 °C steps (70, 72, ...), so 71 °C falls between two marks and no mark shows it.
s: Range -20 °C to 120 °C
Span 140 °C
Smallest division 2 °C
Reading 70 °C
71 °C lies between marks 70 and 72 °C

questions.q:
Read Nikhil's lab record and find what went wrong.
'I held the laboratory thermometer by the bulb and put it in the warm water so the bulb touched the bottom of the beaker. I held it at a slant so I could see the scale. When the column stopped rising I took it out and read 39 °C from above.'
(i)-(iv) Identify four mistakes and, for each, write the correct step.
(v) Which of his mistakes is the one the chapter tells you makes the liquid column fall, and so could have made 39 °C lower than the water's real temperature? Explain.
questions.a: (i) Held by the bulb; a laboratory thermometer must not be held by the bulb. (ii) Bulb touched the bottom; keep the bulb in the water away from the bottom and sides. (iii) Held at a slant; hold it vertically, without tilting. (iv) Took it out and read from above; read it while it is still immersed, with the eye in line with the level of the column. (v) Taking it out before reading: as soon as the thermometer is taken out of the warm water, the level of the liquid column begins to fall, so the value he read can be lower than the water's temperature.
s: Held by the bulb, corrected: do not hold it by the bulb
Bulb touching the bottom, corrected
Tilted, corrected to vertical
Read out of the water and from above, corrected
Taking it out makes the column fall, which can give the low value

questions.q:
Statement 1: The bulb should rest on the bottom of the beaker so that the thermometer stays steady.
Statement 2: While reading, the eye should be directly in line with the level of the liquid column.
Statement 3: The thermometer may be tilted towards the reader, as long as the bulb stays in the water, so that the scale is seen clearly.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: A teacher keeps a laboratory thermometer in water that is boiling over a burner and reads it every two minutes: 97.9 °C, 97.9 °C, 97.9 °C, 97.9 °C. The burner stays on all the time. What do these readings show?
questions.a: The temperature of water stays constant while it is boiling
o: The temperature of water stays constant while it is boiling
The thermometer is stuck, because a heated liquid must keep warming
The burner has stopped heating, because the reading has stopped rising
The water is not really boiling, because boiling water reads exactly 100 °C

questions.q: True or False? 'A student who keeps the thermometer in the water, holds it vertically with the bulb clear of the beaker and waits for the column to stop rising can still record a wrong value if she reads it while looking down at the column from above.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. Keeping it immersed, vertical and clear of the beaker is not enough: while reading, the eye must be directly in line with the level of the liquid column. Looking from above breaks that rule, so the value she notes may not be the mark the column top actually coincides with.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the eye must also be in line with the level of the column; reading from above can give a wrong mark

questions.q:
A Class 6 group dips a laboratory thermometer into a beaker of warm water and reads it, correctly, at these times after dipping:
15 s: 40 °C | 30 s: 52 °C | 45 s: 57 °C | 60 s: 58.5 °C | 75 s: 59 °C | 90 s: 59 °C | 5 min: 56 °C | 10 min: 52 °C
The smallest division of the thermometer is 0.5 °C. Six groups must share this one thermometer in the period.
(a) By which reading was the column no longer rising, and what is the water's temperature?
(b) If a group had read the thermometer at 45 s, how far off would it have been, and why?
(c) Why are the readings at 5 minutes and 10 minutes lower than 59 °C?
(d) To save time, the teacher suggests every group reads at 60 s instead of waiting to see two equal readings (75 s and 90 s). Would you accept this? Use (a) and (b) to weigh the time saved against the accuracy lost.
questions.a: (a) By the 90 s reading: it equals the 75 s reading, 59 °C, so the column had stopped rising (it may have stopped at any time from 60 s to 75 s), and the water was at 59 °C. (b) It would read 57 °C, 2 °C too low, because the column had not yet stopped rising. (c) The water itself cools if you wait too long, so later readings fall below the temperature being measured. (d) Reject it. At 60 s the column was still rising, so the reading of 58.5 °C is one small division (0.5 °C) low, and, worse, a group reading only once at 60 s has no way of knowing whether its column has stopped; with a cooler beaker or another thermometer the error could be bigger, as the 2 °C at 45 s shows. The saving is only 30 s per group, 3 minutes for six groups, which is not worth a reading that may not be the water's temperature.
s: By the 90 s reading (equal to the 75 s one); water at 59 °C
57 °C at 45 s, 2 °C low, column still rising
Later readings fall because the water itself cools
Reject: 0.5 °C low and no check that the column has stopped, for only 3 minutes saved

questions.q: Mitali dips a laboratory thermometer in warm water. The column stops rising after about a minute, but she waits fifteen minutes more 'to be extra accurate' before reading it, keeping it in the water. What is wrong with her plan?
questions.a: The water itself starts to cool, so her reading is lower than at the start
o: The water itself starts to cool, so her reading is lower than at the start
The column keeps rising for fifteen minutes, so her reading is far too high
Nothing is wrong, since a longer wait always gives a more accurate reading
The bulb absorbs all the water's warmth, so the reading falls to zero

questions.q:
Sanjay measures the temperature of warm water. He holds the laboratory thermometer tilted at an angle so that its bulb rests against the side of the beaker, where it stays steady.
(a) Name his two mistakes.
(b) Describe how he should place and hold the thermometer instead.
questions.a: (a) The thermometer is tilted, and its bulb touches the side of the beaker. (b) He should hold it vertically, without tilting, with the bulb immersed in the water but not touching the bottom or the sides of the beaker.
s: Both mistakes: tilted, and bulb touching the side
Correct placing: vertical, bulb in the water clear of the bottom and sides

questions.q: Asif and Lata read the same laboratory thermometer standing upright in a beaker of warm water, at the same moment. Asif stands and looks down at the column and reads 46 °C; Lata bends so that her eye is level with the top of the column and reads 45 °C. Asif says: 'Mine is the better reading, because from above I can see the whole scale clearly.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Both looked at the same column at the same moment, so the water and the column were the same for both; the 1 °C difference comes only from where each eye was. The correct way is to read with the eye directly in line with the level of the liquid column, which is what Lata did, so 45 °C should be recorded. Seeing the whole scale does not help when the eye is not level with the top of the column.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Same column at the same moment, so the 1 °C gap comes from the eye position
The eye must be in line with the column top, so Lata's 45 °C is recorded

questions.q: Four students measure the temperature of warm water in a beaker with a laboratory thermometer. Ali holds it upright with the bulb resting on the bottom of the beaker. Bela holds it tilted, with the bulb in the middle of the water. Charu holds it upright with the bulb in the middle of the water, her eye level with the top of the liquid column. Dev holds it upright with the bulb in the middle of the water, then lifts it out to read it. Who used the correct method?
questions.a: Charu
o: Charu
Ali
Bela
Dev

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After using a laboratory thermometer, Arjun should lay it down gently on the bench rather than drop it into the tray.
Reason (R): If a laboratory thermometer hits against a hard object, it can break.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Six students read the temperature of the same boiling water at a hill-station school: 97.0, 97.2, 96.4, 97.1, 97.2 and 97.1 (all in °C).
(i) Find the highest and lowest readings and the difference between them.
(ii) Which reading stands out from the rest?
(iii) Suggest a mistake in method that could explain it.
(iv) A visitor says, 'Boiling water reads 100 °C, so all six thermometers must be faulty.' Using the readings, reply to the visitor.
(v) Leaving out the odd reading, find the average of the other five and say what value the class should report.
questions.a: (i) Highest 97.2 °C, lowest 96.4 °C, difference 0.8 °C. (ii) 96.4 °C; the other five lie within 0.2 °C of each other. (iii) E.g. it was read after lifting the thermometer out (the column falls), or read with the eye not in line with the column, or with the thermometer tilted. (iv) Five different thermometers, read correctly, agree within 0.2 °C, which would hardly happen if all were faulty; the readings show that these thermometers agree with each other, and only the odd reading of 96.4 °C needs explaining. A reading below 100 °C is not by itself a sign of a fault. (v) (97.0 + 97.2 + 97.1 + 97.2 + 97.1) ÷ 5 = 97.12 °C, so report about 97.1 °C.
s: 97.2, 96.4, difference 0.8 °C
96.4 °C identified as the odd reading
A method mistake from the chapter
Five thermometers agree within 0.2 °C, so they are not all faulty; only 96.4 °C needs explaining
Average 97.12 °C, reported as about 97.1 °C

questions.q: Pooja's beaker holds so little warm water that the bulb of her laboratory thermometer is covered only when it rests on the bottom. What should she do?
questions.a: Add more warm water, so the bulb is covered but clear of the bottom
o: Add more warm water, so the bulb is covered but clear of the bottom
Let the bulb rest on the bottom, since it is at least covered by the water
Tilt the thermometer so that the bulb lies along the water against the side
Dip it for a moment, then take it out and read it quickly before it falls

questions.q:
Five students read the same beaker of warm water, one after another within a minute: 46 °C, 46 °C, 45 °C, 41 °C and 46 °C. Each student held the thermometer vertically with the bulb clear of the bottom and sides, kept the eye level with the top of the column, and read it without lifting it out of the water.
(a) Which reading does not fit the others?
(b) Which step of the correct method did that student most likely miss? Use the reading taken after hers to rule out the water having cooled.
questions.a: (a) 41 °C, which is 4 °C or more below every other reading. (b) She read it before the column had stopped rising, so the liquid had not yet reached the water's temperature. The water had not cooled, because the student after her read 46 °C again.
s: 41 °C picked out as the odd reading
Read before the column stopped rising; the later 46 °C rules out cooling

questions.q: At a hill-station school, a thermometer in water boiling over a burner, read correctly, shows 97.0 °C at 3 minutes. At 9 minutes the water is still boiling and the burner is still on. Read correctly again, the thermometer would show a temperature of ___ K.

A classmate must measure the temperature of hot soup in a tall, narrow steel tumbler, so narrow that the thermometer easily leans against its side. Write three instructions for her. Each instruction must prevent a different mistake that the narrow tumbler makes likely; name the mistake each one prevents.
questions.a: Any three different ones, for example: (1) Hold the thermometer so the bulb is in the middle of the soup, touching neither the side nor the bottom of the tumbler (prevents the bulb resting against the side, which a narrow tumbler invites). (2) Hold it upright with your hand, not leaning against the rim (prevents a tilted thermometer). (3) Bend so that your eye is level with the top of the column above the rim, and read while the bulb is still in the soup (prevents reading from above or lifting it out to see the scale). (4) Hold it by the top of the tube, not by the bulb (prevents holding the bulb when steadying it).
s: First instruction with the mistake it prevents (for example bulb clear of the side and bottom)
Second, different instruction with its mistake (for example held vertically, not leaning)
Third, different instruction with its mistake (for example eye level with the column, read while immersed)

questions.q:
Meera and Arun measure the same beaker of warm water at the same moment with two thermometers. Meera holds hers vertically, bulb clear of the beaker, eye level with the column: 48 °C. Arun holds his tilted and reads along the slant: 50 °C.
(a) Which reading should the group record, and why?
(b) Arun says the 2 °C gap proves Meera's thermometer is faulty. Is that the only explanation? Suggest a test that would settle it.
questions.a: (a) Meera's 48 °C, because she followed the correct way: held vertically, not tilted, with the eye in line with the level of the column. (b) No. Arun's tilted thermometer breaks the rule to hold it vertically, so his method could explain the gap. Test: Arun repeats his reading in the same water with the thermometer held vertically and his eye level with the column (or the two swap thermometers and read correctly); if the readings then agree, the method was the cause.
s: Record 48 °C, taken by the correct method
Not the only explanation: the tilt could cause it; re-read both correctly (or swap) to test

questions.q: At a school in Darjeeling, five students read the same boiling water with the same kind of thermometer: 97.6, 97.7, 97.6, 97.1 and 97.7 °C. Which piece of evidence best shows that the 97.1 °C reading comes from how it was read, not from the water?
questions.a: The other four readings of the same water agree within 0.1 °C
o: The other four readings of the same water agree within 0.1 °C
97.1 °C is lower than 100 °C, the temperature at which water boils
97.1 °C is the lowest of the five readings that were taken
The temperature of boiling water keeps changing while it boils

questions.q:
Arjun wants to check his own fever by putting the bulb of a laboratory thermometer in his mouth, as he would a clinical thermometer.
(a) Name one rule for using a laboratory thermometer that he would find hard to follow while the bulb is in his mouth, and say why.
(b) If he takes it out to read it, what happens to the reading, and so which thermometer should he use?
questions.a: (a) Any one, with its reason: hold it vertically, not tilted (in the mouth it lies at a slant); keep the bulb from touching the sides (it rests against the tongue and cheek); read it while the bulb is still in place with the eye in line with the column (he cannot easily see his own column without a helper or a mirror). (b) As soon as it is taken out, the liquid column begins to fall, so the reading would be too low; he should use a clinical thermometer, which is made for measuring body temperature.
s: Any one rule that mouth placement makes hard (vertical, bulb clear of the sides, read in place with eye in line), with the reason
Column falls once removed, so the reading is low; use a clinical thermometer

questions.q:
At a science fair stall in Kochi, a beaker of fresh tea sits on the table with a laboratory thermometer held upright in it, its bulb clear of the bottom and sides. About 90 visitors are expected in one hour. Procedure P: each visitor bends down and reads the thermometer in the tea, with the eye level with the column; this takes about 40 seconds per visitor. Procedure Q: a student reads the thermometer correctly every minute and writes the value on a board; a visitor just reads the board, about 10 seconds per visitor. Fresh tea is poured in every 15 minutes.
(a) How long would procedure P and procedure Q each take for 90 visitors?
(b) Why must the student in procedure Q bend to read the thermometer while it stays in the tea, rather than lift it up to her eye?
(c) Just after fresh tea is poured in, why should the student not write the first value at once?
(d) Which procedure should the stall use? Justify using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) P: 90 x 40 = 3600 s = 60 minutes; Q: 90 x 10 = 900 s = 15 minutes. (b) The temperature must be read while the thermometer is immersed, because the column begins to fall once it is taken out; and the eye must be in line with the level of the column. (c) The column must first stop rising; a value written before that is lower than the tea's temperature. (d) This one is a real trade-off, and the mark goes to the reasoning. For P, a full answer says that every visitor practises reading a thermometer, the stall's purpose, and admits that 60 minutes leaves no spare time and a careless visitor may lift the thermometer out. For Q, it says that 15 minutes leaves 45 minutes spare and every value is read correctly, and admits that visitors only read a board. A middle plan (P for a few visitors at a time, Q when a queue forms) is also fine if the time is checked.
s: P 60 minutes, Q 15 minutes
Read while immersed (column falls once out), eye in line with the column
Wait for the column to stop rising after a fresh pour
A choice backed by one gain and one cost from (a) to (c): practice for visitors against time and correct values

questions.q:
A group dips a thermometer in warm water and reads it at 15 s: 38 °C, 30 s: 44 °C, 45 s: 46 °C, 60 s: 46 °C and 8 min: 41 °C. Ravi wants to record 38 °C ('the first reading is the freshest'), Neha wants 41 °C ('the longest wait is the most settled').
(a) What value should be recorded?
(b) Explain what is wrong with each of Ravi's and Neha's choices.
questions.a: (a) 46 °C: the 45 s and 60 s readings are equal, so the column had stopped rising. (b) Ravi's 38 °C was taken while the column was still rising, so it had not yet reached the water's temperature. Neha's 41 °C was taken after waiting too long, when the water itself had started to cool.
s: Record 46 °C, where the column stopped rising
38 °C too early (column still rising); 41 °C too late (water cooled)

questions.q:
In a supervised class activity, one laboratory thermometer stands in crushed ice that is melting and another stands in water boiling over a burner. Readings are taken at 0, 3 and 6 minutes.
Ice: 0 °C, 0 °C, 0 °C. Boiling water: 97 °C, 97 °C, 97 °C.
(i) What pattern do both sets of readings show?
(ii) The burner was on all the time. Does that contradict the boiling-water readings? Explain.
(iii) A student read 98 °C at 6 minutes after tilting the thermometer. What should the class do with that reading?
questions.a: (i) Both temperatures stay constant: ice stays at the same temperature while melting, and water stays at the same temperature while boiling. (ii) No; the temperature of water remains constant while it is boiling, even with the burner on. (iii) Treat it as a reading taken by the wrong method (the thermometer must be held vertically) and repeat it correctly, rather than use it.
s: Constant temperature while melting and while boiling
Burner on does not contradict: boiling water stays constant
Tilted reading rejected and repeated with the thermometer vertical

questions.q:
Match each task in Column I with what you should use or look for in Column II.
Column I
1. Checking whether a child has a fever
2. Measuring the temperature of boiling water in the laboratory
3. Getting an approximate idea of the temperature of a hospital ward
4. Knowing the highest air temperature of a town on a given day
Column II
a. A room thermometer on the wall
b. The maximum air temperature in the weather report
c. A clinical thermometer
d. A laboratory thermometer

Rina heard only part of the evening weather report: 'Today the maximum air temperature was 34 °C, and the air temperature varied by 13 °C during the day.'
(a) What was the day's minimum air temperature?
(b) Her brother thinks he heard 'minimum 36 °C'. Explain why that cannot be right for the same day.
questions.a: (a) 34 - 13 = 21 °C. (b) The minimum is the lowest air temperature of the day and the maximum is the highest, so the minimum can never be above the maximum; 36 °C is higher than the 34 °C maximum.
s: Minimum 21 °C
A day's minimum cannot be above its maximum of 34 °C

questions.q:
A library in Pune keeps old manuscripts, which the librarian wants to keep in a room at 28 °C or below. The room thermometer on the wall reads 24 °C at 8 am, 27 °C at 11 am, 30 °C at 2 pm and 29 °C at 5 pm. That day's weather report gives Pune's maximum air temperature as 33 °C and the minimum as 21 °C.
(a) Between which two readings did the room first go above 28 °C?
(b) By how many degrees was the 2 pm room reading below the town's maximum for the day?
(c) Why should the librarian use the room thermometer, rather than the weather report, to decide about the manuscripts?
(d) Tomorrow is forecast to be similar. Should she move the manuscripts to a cooler room at 11 am, or wait until the room thermometer passes 28 °C? Justify using (a) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Between 11 am (27 °C) and 2 pm (30 °C). (b) 33 - 30 = 3 °C. (c) The room thermometer gives an approximate idea of the temperature of that room, which is what matters for the manuscripts; the report gives only the town's highest and lowest air temperature of the day. (d) Move them at 11 am. At 11 am the room was only 1 °C below the limit and it rose 3 °C in the next three hours, passing 28 °C, so on a similar day it will very likely cross again. Waiting for the thermometer to pass 28 °C means the manuscripts are already above the limit when she acts, and a room thermometer gives only an approximate idea, so she may not catch the moment. Moving early costs some effort on a day that might stay cooler, a small price against harm to old manuscripts.
s: Between 11 am and 2 pm
3 °C below the town's maximum
Room thermometer describes this room; the report describes the town's daily extremes
Move at 11 am: 1 °C margin and a 3 °C rise by 2 pm; waiting means acting only after the limit is passed

questions.q: Lakshmi records the weather report for 10 days. Day 1: maximum 29 °C, minimum 14 °C. Day 10: maximum 36 °C, minimum 21 °C. On most days in between, both values crept up, though they fell on a couple of days. Which season is most likely approaching?
questions.a: Summer, since both values generally rise over the ten days
o: Summer, since both values generally rise over the ten days
Winter, since every minimum is lower than its maximum
Neither, since the values did not rise on every single day
Winter, since the maximum and minimum differ by 15 °C

questions.q:
A student in Shimla recorded the weather report for six successive days in October.
Maximum (°C): 21, 19, 20, 18, 17, 16
Minimum (°C): 10, 8, 9, 6, 6, 5
(i) On which day was the gap between the maximum and the minimum largest, and how large was it?
(ii) Did the minimum fall on every day? Support your answer from the data.
(iii) Which season is approaching? Give one piece of evidence and explain why the days that did not fall do not change your answer.
questions.a: (i) Gaps: 11, 11, 11, 12, 11, 11 °C, so day 4, with 18 - 6 = 12 °C. (ii) No: it rose from 8 °C to 9 °C on day 3 and stayed at 6 °C on day 5, though it fell on the other days. (iii) Winter: the maximum fell from 21 °C to 16 °C (or the minimum from 10 °C to 5 °C). Weather depends on several factors, so temperatures vary every day; the fall towards winter is a general trend, not a fall every day.
s: Day 4, gap 12 °C
Minimum rose on day 3 and stayed level on day 5
Winter, with evidence; daily variation does not break the general trend

questions.q: A farmer near Ludhiana reads a weather forecast that gives the minimum air temperatures for the next four nights as 8 °C, 6 °C, 4 °C and 3 °C. His young plants are harmed below 5 °C. What should he do?
questions.a: Plan to cover the plants from the third night, the first below 5 °C
o: Plan to cover the plants from the third night, the first below 5 °C
Do nothing for now, since the first night's minimum of 8 °C is well above 5 °C
Cover the plants only on the fourth night, because that is the coldest one
Ignore the forecast, since air temperatures vary every day and a forecast cannot help

questions.q:
At 11 am the room thermometer in a school laboratory in Agra reads 27 °C. On the evening news, the town's maximum air temperature for the day is given as 33 °C.
(a) Does the 27 °C reading show that the news was wrong? Explain.
(b) A student wants to describe how hot the day was in Agra for her diary. Which of the two numbers should she use, and why?
questions.a: (a) No. The room thermometer gives an approximate idea of the temperature of that one room at 11 am, while 33 °C is the highest air temperature of the town during the whole day; they describe different things. (b) The weather report's maximum, 33 °C, because it describes the town's air for the whole day, not one room at one moment.
s: Not a contradiction: one room at one time against the town's highest air temperature of the day
Use 33 °C, the town's daily maximum, with the reason

questions.q: On a room thermometer in a clinic, the bigger marks are 10 °C apart with 5 small divisions between them. At 9 am the top of the liquid column is 3 small divisions above the 20 °C mark; at 1 pm it is 2 small divisions above the 30 °C mark. The room warmed by about ___ °C.

True or False? 'The weather report gave the day's maximum as 34 °C and the minimum as 21 °C, so at some time that day the air temperature was 13 °C.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. 13 °C is the difference between the maximum and the minimum (34 - 21 = 13 °C), not a temperature the air reached. The minimum, 21 °C, is the lowest air temperature of the day, so the air never fell to 13 °C; it stayed between 21 °C and 34 °C.
s: Verdict: False
13 °C is the gap 34 - 21; the air stayed between 21 °C and 34 °C

questions.q:
A school in Hyderabad must choose a day next week for its sports day. The forecast maximum air temperatures are: Monday 36 °C, Tuesday 36 °C, Wednesday 37 °C, Thursday 33 °C, Friday 35 °C. The principal's rule is: no sports day on a day forecast above 35 °C, and she wants the chosen day to be at least 1 °C below that limit, because forecasts can be off. Thursday clashes with a unit test that can be moved only with difficulty.
(a) Which days satisfy the principal's rule?
(b) How far below the limit is each of those days?
(c) Why might the actual maximum on the chosen day differ from the forecast?
(d) Choose a day and justify it, weighing the temperatures against the unit-test clash.
questions.a: (a) Thursday (33 °C) and Friday (35 °C); Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday are above 35 °C. (b) Thursday is 2 °C below the limit; Friday is exactly at it, 0 °C below. (c) Weather depends on several factors, so air temperature varies from day to day and the actual value can differ from the forecast. (d) Thursday. Friday is tempting because the test need not move, but it sits exactly on the 35 °C limit, with none of the 1 °C margin the principal asked for, and (c) shows the actual maximum can go above the forecast. Thursday's 2 °C margin is the only safe one, and a unit test can be moved, with difficulty, while a hot sports day cannot be undone.
s: Thursday and Friday only
Thursday 2 °C below, Friday at the limit
Daily variation with weather factors
Thursday: Friday has no margin and the forecast can be exceeded; the test can be moved

questions.q:
Find the error. A Class 6 group in Bhubaneswar records the weather report for seven days (maximum, minimum, in °C):
Day 1: 30, 18 | Day 2: 31, 19 | Day 3: 17, 32 | Day 4: 33, 20 | Day 5: 32, 20 | Day 6: 34, 21 | Day 7: 35, 22
(a) Which day's entry must contain an error? Give the reason.
(b) Leaving that day out, find the average maximum of the other six days.
(c) If the two values for that day were simply written in the wrong order, what would the corrected maximum list be, and on which day would the maximum fall?
(d) Should the group swap the two values for that day or leave the day out of their analysis? Weigh how well the swapped values fit the neighbouring days.
questions.a: (a) Day 3: the maximum (17 °C) is lower than the minimum (32 °C), which cannot happen, since the maximum is the highest air temperature of the day. (b) (30 + 31 + 33 + 32 + 34 + 35) ÷ 6 = 195 ÷ 6 = 32.5 °C. (c) 30, 31, 32, 33, 32, 34, 35 °C; it would fall only on day 5 (33 to 32 °C), within a general rise. (d) Leave day 3 out (or mark it doubtful). A swap is tempting because a maximum of 32 °C fits neatly between 31 °C and 33 °C, but the swapped minimum of 17 °C would be below both day 1 (18 °C) and day 2 (19 °C) while the other minimums rise steadily, so only one of the two values fits and the swap cannot be confirmed. Leaving the day out costs little: the other six days still show the maximum rising from 30 °C to 35 °C.
s: Day 3: maximum below minimum is impossible
Average 32.5 °C
Corrected list; maximum falls only on day 5
Leave day 3 out: 32 °C fits but 17 °C does not, and six days still show the rise
